content:
Claude Code auto mode becomes the default permission setting for users starting today.

Pro, Max, and Team user sessions will default to auto mode, unless users or admins have locked other settings.

Anthropic is no longer charging for the extra tokens generated by each tool call from the auto mode classifier.

Anthropic noted that auto mode replaces repeated authorization prompts with a classifier, which checks for irreversible, destructive, or out-of-bounds operations on every tool call.

If the classifier blocks an operation, Claude can attempt to perform it in a safer way or request authorization; if blocked multiple times in a row, the session reverts to manual approval.

As part of this change, Anthropic said it stopped charging for the "small amount of extra tokens" used by the auto mode classifier last week.

Anthropic noted that in a study of 1,053 paid testers, humans identified only 13.6% of dangerous instructions, while auto mode achieved 89%. After 50 prompts, human performance dropped to about 5%.

However, Anthropic also cautioned that the classifier cannot completely eliminate risk, and recommended retaining human review for changes in production environments.

This shift makes Claude Code's long-running jobs more practical, working with existing routines, voice mode, and the built-in browser in the Mac version. Anthropic said Team and Enterprise customers' auto mode users submitted roughly 25% more pull requests.

9to5Mac's take

Although it sounds risky, for experienced users this default setting should be the right choice. However, users should still build a certain level of trust with the coding agent before relying on auto mode.

It is also quite interesting that Anthropic is taking this step. By comparison, OpenAI at one point chose not to use auto mode in its most powerful GPT-5.6 version for added safety.
